{"source":"The museum tested a new wayfinding sheet during four afternoon sessions in June. Visitors received a single folded page at the entrance, with a simple map on one side and room names on the other. The old sheet had listed exhibits alphabetically. Staff suspected that visitors were using it as a checklist rather than a route, but they had no direct evidence of that behavior. For the trial, volunteers offered the new sheet to every third arriving group when the entrance was not crowded. Thirty-six groups accepted it; nine declined. The volunteers did not track groups that arrived during busy periods, so the figures do not describe all visitors. At the exit, twenty accepted groups answered one question about finding the textile gallery. Fifteen said it had been easy, three said it had been difficult, and two were unsure. There was no comparison question for visitors using the old sheet. One volunteer also noticed that several families paused at the stairwell and checked the map twice. Her observation is useful for locating a possible trouble spot, though it does not establish how often the problem occurred. The design team proposes moving the textile gallery arrow closer to the stairwell symbol and testing that change in July. They also want to ask the same exit question of groups using each sheet. If staffing allows, a volunteer will record how many groups skip the sheet entirely. The museum can print another small batch for the July test without changing its permanent signs. A larger print run should wait until staff can compare the two sheets under similar conditions.
